{{short description|American mathematician and computer architect}}
'''Daniel Leonid Slotnick''' (November 12, 1931 – October 25, 1985) was an American [[mathematician]] and [[Computer architecture|computer architect]].

== Education and career ==
Slotnick studied Mathematics at [[Columbia University]], where he obtained a Bachelor's in 1951 and a Master's in 1952.

In 1956 he obtained a PhD at the [[Courant Institute School of Mathematics, Computing, and Data Science|Courant Institute]] of Mathematical Sciences of [[New York University]], supervised by [[Jürgen K. Moser]] and [[Kurt Otto Friedrichs]].

He worked as professor of computer science at the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign|University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign.]]

He was awarded the [[American Federation of Information Processing Societies|AFIPS]] Prize in 1962 and was elected an [[Lists of fellows of the IEEE|IEEE Fellow]] in 1976.

Slotnick died in [[Baltimore, Maryland]], on October 25, 1985, age 53, from an apparent heart attack while jogging.<ref>{{cite web | title=High-Speed Computer Builder Daniel Slotnick | website=[[Chicago Tribune]] | date=29 October 1985 | url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1985/10/29/high-speed-computer-builder-daniel-slotnick/ }}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |date=1985-10-31 |title=Daniel L. Slotnick, 53, Dies; Designed a NASA Computer |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1985/10/31/us/daniel-l-slotnick-53-dies-designed-a-nasa-computer.html |access-date=2026-08-19 |work=[[The New York Times]] |language=en-US |issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

In 1985, when the [[Institute for Defense Analyses]] and [[National Security Agency]] formed their supercomputing research facility in the [[Washington, D.C.]] area, Slotnick's widow donated his library to them. In 1987 the first issue of ''[[The Journal of Supercomputing]]'' contained a tribute to Slotnick.

== Research activities ==
Slotnick, in papers published with [[John Cocke (computer scientist)|John Cocke]] in 1958, discussed the use of [[parallel computing|parallelism]] in numerical calculations for the first time. He later served as the chief architect of the [[ILLIAC IV]] supercomputer.<ref>
{{Citation | last1=Schneck | first1=Paul | title=Dedication. Daniel L. Slotnick, 1931 to 1985 | doi=10.1007/BF00138601 | year=1987 | journal=The Journal of Supercomputing | issn=0920-8542 | volume=1 | issue=1 | pages=5–6| s2cid=218841256 }}.</ref>

He was the principal investigator on a [[DARPA]] contract in the early 1970s that produced the ILLIAC IV and the [[ARPANET]]. It was a fairly large operation, with its own building on the [[University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign]] campus, originally called the Center for Advanced Computation but which is now the Astronomy Building. ILLIAC IV was constructed by the [[Burroughs Corporation]], using special chips made by [[Fairchild Semiconductor]]. Because of campus unrest due to the [[Vietnam War|Vietnam war]], and [[Mike Mansfield#The Mansfield Amendments|the Mansfield amendments]], the ILLIAC IV was completed and installed at [[Ames Research Center]] instead of the University of Illinois, and Slotnick's DARPA contract was not renewed.

==ARPANET==
Most of the development of the ARPANET took place at [[MIT Lincoln Laboratory]] and [[Raytheon BBN|BBN Technologies]]. However, it was planned that ILLIAC IV would be on the network, and some work was funded by Slotnick's DARPA contract. For example, a standard character set was established, and also the [[George B. Purdy#Purdy polynomial|Purdy polynomial]], a secure hash function to protect passwords on ARPANET. Ironically, when the ILLIAC IV project was moved to [[Ames Research Center]], the computer could only be accessed by telephone.
